questions.prompt: What is compound interest?
choices: Interest earned on your original money AND on the interest it has already earned
Interest paid only on the money you first put in
A one-time bonus banks give new customers
A fee charged when you withdraw savings
questions.explanation: Compound interest means your interest earns interest too. Over time that snowball effect makes your money grow faster and faster.

questions.prompt: Compound interest can also work against you when you carry a balance on a credit card.
questions.explanation: Debt compounds too. Unpaid interest gets added to what you owe, so the balance you're charged interest on keeps growing.

questions.prompt: You invest $1,000 at 10% compounded once a year. How many dollars do you have after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Year 1: $1,000 grows to $1,100. Year 2: that $1,100 grows to $1,210 — the extra $10 is interest earning interest.

questions.prompt: You put $1,000 in two accounts at the same 10% rate. Which ends up with more after several years?
choices: The compound-interest account
The simple-interest account
They always tie exactly
Neither earns anything
questions.explanation: Simple interest pays only on your original $1,000 each year. Compound interest pays on the growing balance, so it pulls ahead and the gap widens over time.

questions.prompt: Match each compound-interest term to its meaning.
pairs: The original amount you invest or borrow
The percentage your money grows each period
The total amount your account is worth right now
questions.explanation: Principal is your starting money, the rate is how fast it grows, compounding is interest on interest, and the balance is the running total.

questions.prompt: Which of these make compound interest work harder for you? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Starting as early as you can
Leaving your earnings invested instead of spending them
A higher interest rate
Withdrawing your interest every year
questions.explanation: More time, reinvested earnings, and a higher rate all feed the snowball. Cashing out your interest every year stops it from compounding.

questions.prompt: Put these interest rates in order by how much a $1,000 investment earns over 10 years, least to most.
questions.explanation: A higher rate compounds faster, so the higher the rate the more interest you pile up over the same 10 years.

questions.prompt: What does the Rule of 72 help you estimate?
choices: Roughly how many years it takes your money to double
Exactly how much tax you'll owe
The best stock to buy
How much to spend each month
questions.explanation: Divide 72 by your yearly interest rate and you get a quick estimate of how many years it takes an investment to double.

questions.prompt: At an 8% yearly return, about how many years does it take your money to double?
questions.explanation: 72 ÷ 8 = 9. So money growing at 8% a year doubles in roughly 9 years.

questions.prompt: Match each yearly return to its approximate doubling time using the Rule of 72.
You want your money to double in about 6 years. Roughly what yearly return do you need?
questions.explanation: Flip the rule around: 72 ÷ 6 years = 12%. You'd need about a 12% yearly return.

questions.prompt: The Rule of 72 can also estimate how fast rising prices (inflation) cut your money's value in half.
questions.explanation: The same math works for anything that grows by a percentage — including inflation eating away at what your dollars can buy.

questions.prompt: At a 3% yearly return, about how long does it take money to double?
choices: 24 years
12 years
6 years
36 years
questions.explanation: 72 ÷ 3 = 24. Low returns mean a long wait — about 24 years to double at 3%.

questions.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, sort each yearly return by how long it takes money to double.
When it comes to growing wealth, what usually matters most?
choices: How early you start, because time lets money compound
Picking the single perfect stock
Being born rich
Waiting until you earn a lot before you invest
questions.explanation: Time is the secret ingredient. The earlier you start, the more years compounding has to turn small amounts into a lot.

questions.prompt: Someone who invests from age 18 to 28 and then stops can end up with more than someone who starts at 28 and invests for decades.
questions.explanation: This is the classic early-saver surprise: the head start gives the early investor's money extra years to compound, which can beat a bigger total invested later.

questions.prompt: Early Erin invests $200 a month for 10 years, then stops. How many dollars did she personally put in?
questions.explanation: $200 × 12 months × 10 years = $24,000. That's all Erin ever contributes — the rest of her growth comes from compounding.

questions.prompt: Late Liam invests $200 a month from age 28 to 65 — that's 37 years. How many dollars does he personally put in?
questions.explanation: $200 × 12 × 37 = $88,800. Liam contributes far more than Erin, yet her early start can still put her ahead.

questions.prompt: Why can an early starter end up ahead even after investing fewer total dollars?
choices: Their money has many more years to compound
Early investors get a secret higher rate
Banks reward youth with free money
Older investors pay a penalty
questions.explanation: Extra decades of compounding do the heavy lifting. Time in the market beats the amount you put in.

questions.prompt: Which habits help you take full advantage of time? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Start investing as early as possible
Invest consistently, even small amounts
Leave your money invested to keep compounding
Wait many years before you begin
questions.explanation: Start early, stay consistent, and let it ride — those three give compounding the years it needs. Waiting just throws that time away.

questions.prompt: Put these savers in order by the total dollars they personally contribute, least to most.
questions.explanation: $24,000 vs $48,000 vs $88,800. Erin puts in the least — yet starting first gives her money the most time to grow.

questions.prompt: What is dollar-cost averaging?
choices: Investing a fixed dollar amount on a regular schedule, no matter the price
Investing everything you have the moment you get it
Only buying when prices are at their lowest
Selling a little bit every month
questions.explanation: You put in the same amount on a set schedule — say $100 every month — regardless of whether prices are up or down.

questions.prompt: With dollar-cost averaging, a fixed amount of money buys more shares when the price is low and fewer when it's high.
questions.explanation: Because your dollars are fixed, a lower price stretches further and buys more shares — automatically leaning into cheap prices.

questions.prompt: You invest $120 this month and the share price is $12. How many shares do you buy?
Next month you invest another $120, but the price has dropped to $6. How many shares do you buy now?
questions.explanation: $120 ÷ $6 = 20 shares. The same $120 bought twice as many shares because the price fell.

questions.prompt: Over those two months you invested $240 and now own 30 shares. What average price did you pay per share?
questions.explanation: $240 ÷ 30 shares = $8 per share — lower than the simple average of $12 and $6 ($9), because you bought more shares when cheap.

questions.prompt: Which are real benefits of dollar-cost averaging? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: It takes the pressure off trying to time the market perfectly
It automatically buys more shares when prices are low
It builds a steady investing habit
It guarantees you'll never lose money
questions.explanation: DCA removes timing stress, leans into low prices, and builds discipline — but no strategy guarantees a profit.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to set up a dollar-cost averaging plan.
items: Pick an amount you can invest regularly
Choose a fixed schedule, like every month
Invest that amount every period no matter the price
Keep it going through the ups and downs
questions.explanation: Decide the amount, set the schedule, invest on autopilot, and stay consistent — that's dollar-cost averaging.

questions.prompt: In a SMART goal, what does the 'M' stand for?
choices: Measurable
Money
Maximum
Mandatory
questions.explanation: Measurable means you can track progress with a number — like saving $1,200 — so you know when you've hit it.

questions.prompt: Match each letter of SMART to what it stands for.
questions.explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound — clear targets you can actually reach.

questions.prompt: Sort each goal by whether you'd keep the money safe in savings or invest it for growth.
items: College fund for a baby born today
questions.explanation: Money you need soon should stay safe in savings; money you won't touch for years can be invested to grow and ride out the ups and downs.

questions.prompt: Money you'll need in just a few months is best put in stocks so it can grow as much as possible.
questions.explanation: Stocks can drop right when you need the cash. Short-term money belongs somewhere safe, like a savings account.

questions.prompt: Why invest rather than just save for a goal that's decades away?
choices: You have time to ride out market dips and let compounding grow your money
Savings accounts are illegal for long goals
Investing has no risk over long periods
It's the only way to open an account
questions.explanation: A long time horizon lets you weather market ups and downs and gives compounding years to work — so growth investments make sense.

questions.prompt: Your SMART goal is to save $1,200 for a laptop in 12 months. How many dollars must you save each month?
questions.explanation: $1,200 ÷ 12 months = $100 a month. Breaking a goal into monthly steps makes it Achievable and Time-bound.

questions.prompt: Which of these make a goal 'SMART'? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: It's specific and measurable
It has a clear deadline
It's realistic for your income
It's vague, like 'save more someday'
questions.explanation: SMART goals are clear, have a deadline, and are realistic. 'Save more someday' is too fuzzy to act on or track.

questions.prompt: Which best describes compound interest?
choices: Earning interest on both your original money and the interest already earned
Earning interest only on your original deposit
A flat fee added to your account each year
A discount for keeping money in the bank
questions.explanation: Compound interest snowballs because your earnings start earning too — the engine behind long-term growth.

questions.prompt: You invest $500 at 10% compounded once a year. How many dollars do you have after 2 years?
questions.explanation: Year 1: $500 → $550. Year 2: $550 → $605. The extra $5 is interest earning interest.

questions.prompt: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at a 6% yearly return?
questions.explanation: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. Divide 72 by the rate for a quick doubling estimate.

questions.prompt: Compounding only helps you — it never works against you.
questions.explanation: Debt compounds too. Unpaid credit-card interest grows the same way, which is why balances can balloon fast.

questions.prompt: Why can someone who starts investing at 18 beat someone who starts at 28, even with less money invested?
choices: Their money has more years to compound
They secretly earn a higher interest rate
Young people pay no taxes
Older investors are charged extra fees
questions.explanation: Time in the market is the edge. Extra years of compounding can outweigh a larger amount invested later.

questions.prompt: With dollar-cost averaging you invest $120 and the share price is $8. How many shares do you buy?
questions.explanation: $120 ÷ $8 = 15 shares. A fixed dollar amount buys more shares when the price is lower.

questions.prompt: Sort each goal by whether you'd save the money or invest it for growth.
questions.explanation: Near-term money stays safe in savings; far-off goals can be invested so compounding and growth have time to work.

questions.prompt: Match each letter of a SMART goal to what it stands for.
questions.explanation: SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound — clear enough to act on and track.

questions.prompt: Which choices help you harness the power of time and compounding? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Start investing early
Reinvest your earnings instead of spending them
Invest consistently over the years
Withdraw your gains every few months
questions.explanation: Starting early, reinvesting, and staying consistent all feed the compounding snowball. Cashing out often cuts it short.

questions.prompt: Put these $1,000 investments in order by their ending value after 10 years, least to most.
questions.explanation: A higher rate compounds faster, so over the same 10 years the 10% investment grows the most and the 2% grows the least.
